paragraphs: We have tested the principle of legislation for States, or communities, in their political capacities by our own experiment, and the result shows where it leads. The fate of every other confederate government we know of shows the same thing, in exact proportion to how far the principle prevailed in each. These confirmations deserve a separate and careful examination. For now I will merely observe that, of all the confederacies of antiquity that history has handed down to us, the Lycian and Achaean leagues appear, as far as traces of them survive, to have been the freest from the fetters of this mistaken principle. They were accordingly the ones that political writers have most deservedly and most generously praised.

This objectionable principle may be called, as truly as emphatically, the parent of anarchy. We have seen that delinquencies in the members of the Union are its natural and necessary offspring, that the only constitutional remedy when they occur is force, and that the immediate result of using force is civil war.

It remains to ask how far so odious an engine of government, applied to us, could even achieve its end. Suppose there were no large army constantly at the disposal of the national government. Then it would either be unable to use force at all, or, if it did use it, the result would be a war between parts of the Confederacy over infractions of a league. In such a war the strongest combination would be the most likely to win, whether it was made up of those who supported the general authority or of those who resisted it. It would rarely happen that the delinquency to be corrected was confined to a single member. If more than one had neglected their duty, their similar situation would lead them to unite in common defense. Apart from this motive of sympathy, suppose a large and influential State were the offender. It would commonly have enough weight with its neighbors to win some of them over as allies. Specious arguments of danger to the common liberty could easily be contrived, and plausible excuses for the offender's failures could readily be invented. These would alarm the fears, inflame the passions, and win the good will even of States that were not guilty of any violation or omission of duty. This would be the more likely because the delinquencies of the larger members might sometimes be expected to come from the ambitious calculation of their rulers, who wanted to be rid of all outside control over their plans for personal aggrandizement. To carry out those plans better, it is to be presumed that they would first tamper with leading individuals in the neighboring States. If allies could not be found at home, they would turn to foreign powers, who would seldom be unwilling to encourage the dissensions of a Confederacy whose firm union they had so much reason to fear. Once the sword is drawn, the passions of men observe no bounds of moderation. Wounded pride and irritated resentment would tend to drive the States against which the arms of the Union were used to any extreme needed to avenge the insult or to avoid the disgrace of submission. The first war of this kind would probably end in the dissolution of the Union.

We may regard this as the violent death of the Confederacy. Its more natural death is the one we now seem about to suffer, unless the federal system is quickly renewed in a more substantial form. Given the character of this country, it is not likely that the complying States would often be inclined to support the authority of the Union by making war on the non-complying States. They would always be readier to take the milder course of putting themselves on an equal footing with the delinquent members by following their example. In this way the guilt of all would become the security of all. Our past experience has shown this spirit at work in its full light. There would in fact be an insuperable difficulty in deciding when force could properly be used. Take money contributions, the most usual source of delinquency. It would often be impossible to decide whether a State had failed to pay because it was unwilling or because it was unable. The plea of inability would always be at hand. The case would have to be flagrant indeed for the falseness of that plea to be detected with enough certainty to justify the harsh expedient of compulsion. It is easy to see that this problem alone, each time it arose, would open a wide field for factional views, bias, and oppression in whatever majority happened to prevail in the national council.

It hardly takes any effort to prove that the States should not prefer a national Constitution that could be kept in motion only by a large army continually on foot to carry out the ordinary requisitions or decrees of the government. Yet that is the plain alternative for those who want to deny it the power of reaching individuals. Such a scheme, if it could work at all, would instantly degenerate into a military despotism. But it will be found impracticable in every light. The resources of the Union would not be equal to maintaining an army large enough to hold the larger States to their duty, and the means to raise such an army in the first place would never be provided. Consider the population and strength of several of these States singly at the present moment, and look ahead to what they will become even half a century from now. Whoever does so will at once dismiss as idle and visionary any scheme that aims to regulate their movements by laws operating on them in their collective capacities, and executed by a coercion applicable to them in the same capacities. A project of this kind is little less romantic than the monster-taming spirit attributed to the fabled heroes and demigods of antiquity.

Even in confederacies made up of members smaller than many of our counties, the principle of legislation for sovereign States, backed by military coercion, has never been found effective. It has rarely been tried except against the weaker members. In most instances, attempts to coerce the refractory and disobedient have been the signal for bloody wars in which one half of the confederacy raised its banners against the other half.

An intelligent mind must draw this clear conclusion from these observations. If a federal government capable of regulating the common concerns and preserving the general tranquillity can be built at all, it must be founded, as to the objects committed to its care, on the reverse of the principle that the opponents of the proposed Constitution contend for. It must carry its agency to the persons of the citizens. It must need no intermediate legislations, but must itself be empowered to use the arm of the ordinary public official to carry out its own resolutions. The majesty of the national authority must be displayed through the courts of justice. The government of the Union, like that of each State, must be able to address itself directly to the hopes and fears of individuals, and to enlist in its support the passions that have the strongest hold on the human heart. In short, it must have all the means, and the right to use all the methods, of carrying out the powers entrusted to it that the governments of the particular States have and use.

Perhaps it will be objected to this reasoning that if any State were disaffected toward the authority of the Union, it could at any time obstruct the execution of the Union's laws. That would bring the matter to the same issue of force, whose necessity is held against the opposite scheme.

This objection loses its plausibility the moment we notice the essential difference between mere NON-COMPLIANCE and DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE. If a measure of the Union needs the intervention of the State legislatures to take effect, they have only NOT TO ACT, or TO ACT EVASIVELY, and the measure is defeated. This neglect of duty may be disguised under affected but insubstantial provisions, so that it does not appear and so does not alarm the people for the safety of the Constitution. The State leaders may even claim credit for their sly invasions of it, on the ground of some temporary convenience, exemption, or advantage.

But suppose the execution of the laws of the national government did not require the intervention of the State legislatures, and the laws took effect directly on the citizens themselves. Then the particular governments could not interrupt their progress without an open and violent exercise of unconstitutional power. No omissions or evasions would do. The States would be obliged to act, and to act in a way that left no doubt they had encroached on the national rights. An experiment of this nature would always be hazardous in the face of a constitution at all able to defend itself, and of a people enlightened enough to tell a legal exercise of authority from an illegal usurpation. To succeed, it would require not merely a factional majority in the legislature but the concurrence of the courts of justice and of the body of the people. If the judges were not part of a conspiracy with the legislature, they would pronounce the resolutions of such a majority contrary to the supreme law of the land, unconstitutional, and void. If the people were not infected with the spirit of their State representatives, they would act as the natural guardians of the Constitution. They would throw their weight into the national scale and give it a decided advantage in the contest. Such attempts would not often be made lightly or rashly, because they could seldom be made without danger to their authors, except when the federal authority was being used tyrannically.

Suppose instead that opposition to the national government arose from the disorderly conduct of refractory or seditious individuals. It could be overcome by the same means that are used every day against the same evil under the State governments. The civil authorities are equally ministers of the law of the land, whatever its source, and they would doubtless be as ready to protect national regulations as local ones from the inroads of private license. Consider the partial commotions and insurrections that sometimes disturb society, arising from the intrigues of an inconsiderable faction or from sudden or occasional ill humors that do not infect the great body of the community. The general government could command more extensive resources for putting down disturbances of that kind than any single member could. Then there are the mortal feuds that at certain junctures spread a conflagration through a whole nation or a very large part of it. They may come from weighty causes of discontent given by the government, or from the contagion of some violent popular fit. They do not fall within any ordinary rules of calculation. When they happen, they commonly amount to revolutions and dismemberments of empire. No form of government can always avoid or control them. It is vain to hope to guard against events too mighty for human foresight or precaution, and it would be idle to object to a government because it could not perform impossibilities.
